content.text: I have solid black-box data. Network is unavailable (DNS fails for pypi.org / readthedocs / githubusercontent, no proxy) and bidict is not installed locally, so the documentation portion comes from my knowledge of bidict's published API docs — I'll tag every claim by evidence class.

input.dimension: bidict library behaviour (black-box + public API contract) for the JS port

findings.rule: bidict({'a':1,'b':2,'c':3}) constructs without error (all keys and all values distinct). 'a' in b -> True; 3 in b.inv -> True. Each `in` result is printed with Python bool str: exactly 'True\n' / 'False\n'.
Forward membership covers every literal key ('a','b','c'); inverse membership covers every literal value (1,2,3). No cross-talk.
The two membership tests are fully independent: key 'c' pairs with value 3, but result1/result2 are computed separately, so pairing is irrelevant.
b.inv's key set is exactly {1,2,3}; 0 is absent. b.inv.__contains__ tests the ORIGINAL VALUES, i.e. keys of the inverse.
Key lookup is exact/case-sensitive string identity (Python dict hashing of str). 'A' != 'a'. No normalization, folding, or coercion.
Types are not coerced across directions: the str '1' is not a key of b even though int 1 is a key of b.inv. Forward keyspace is str-only, inverse keyspace is int-only.
No prefix/substring/partial matching in either direction; membership is whole-key equality only.
Absent key and absent value both yield False; missing membership never raises (unlike b[k] which would raise KeyError).
bidict does NOT strip whitespace from keys: ' a' is a distinct key from 'a' and is absent. (Contrast with int() for --val, which does strip.)
Keys with embedded control characters are compared byte-exactly; 'a\n' is not 'a'. Output is still exactly two lines, so a trailing newline in the key never leaks into stdout.
Empty-string key is a legal, hashable lookup that simply returns False — it does not raise and is not treated as 'missing argument'.
Non-ASCII keys are handled as Unicode codepoint sequences and compared exactly; no encoding error, no NFC/NFD folding to 'e'.
Inverse membership happens AFTER argparse's int() conversion: int('01') == 1, which is a value of b -> True. The JS port must compare the parsed integer, not the raw string.
int('+3') == 3 -> present in b.inv. Numeric normalization is done by the int conversion, not by bidict.

int('1_0') == 10, which is NOT a value of b -> False. A JS port using Number('1_0') would produce NaN and, if NaN were then looked up, could still print False by accident — but for e.g. '1_0' vs '10' equivalence the port must implement Python int() underscore rules before the membership test.
Confirms 10 is genuinely absent from b.inv (so case '1_0' is a real value-space miss, not a parse failure).
int(' 2 ') == 2 -> present in b.inv. Surrounding ASCII whitespace is stripped by int(), so the inverse lookup sees 2.
int('-0') == 0 -> absent. Python has no negative-zero int; a JS port must not let -0 vs 0 (or -0 stringification) change the lookup result.

surprises: `in` on a bidict checks KEYS ONLY, never values — even though the mapping is bidirectional. The only way to test the value side is `v in b.inv`. This is proven here: `--key 1 --val 1` gives False/True, so int 1 is reachable only through the inverse. A naive JS port that made `has()` check both directions would silently pass most of this script's cases and fail on `--key 1`/`--key 2`/`--key 3`.

`b.values()` is documented to return a set-like KeysView (of the inverse), NOT a dict_values — because bidict values are unique. So `b.values()` supports O(1) `in`, set operators, and compares equal to a set. This differs from every dict-shaped intuition a JS porter would have.

bidict is NOT a dict subclass (documented). `isinstance(b, dict)` is False; it implements the Mapping/BidirectionalMapping ABCs instead. Anything in a sibling script that branches on dict-ness will differ.

KeyAndValueDuplicationError multiply inherits from BOTH KeyDuplicationError and ValueDuplicationError. JS has single inheritance, so a faithful port needs `Symbol.hasInstance` on one of the two parents to keep `instanceof` truthful for both.

Re-putting an item that is already present verbatim (same key AND same value) is a no-op and does NOT raise, even under the strictest ON_DUP_RAISE policy. Only a duplicate that would collide with a *different* existing item raises.

OrderedBidict.__eq__ is order-INSENSITIVE (matching dict); order-sensitive comparison requires the explicit equals_order_sensitive() method. So `OrderedBidict([(1,2),(3,4)]) == OrderedBidict([(3,4),(1,2)])` is True.

Mutating through `b.inv` mutates `b` — the inverse is a live cross-linked view, not a snapshot copy. `b.inv.inv is b` is an identity guarantee, so the port must cross-link two objects, not regenerate the inverse on each property access.

Environment/probing caveat (not a bidict fact): this sandbox's filesystem showed stale reads when the SAME temp file was overwritten by consecutive fast runs and immediately inspected with od — one batch produced results shifted by a run and two apparently-empty outputs. Every case above was re-verified writing to a UNIQUE file per invocation. Any differential test harness for the JS port must use per-case output files (or read stdout via a pipe) or it will chase phantom mismatches.

No network in this sandbox (DNS resolution fails for pypi.org, bidict.readthedocs.io and raw.githubusercontent.com; all *_proxy vars are empty) and bidict is not installed under /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages, so the documentation half of this dimension could not be live-fetched; it is reconstructed from knowledge of the published docs and each claim below is tagged by evidence class.
jsImplementationNotes: [PROVENANCE / INFER] The bundled library is bidict 0.23.x, almost certainly 0.23.1 (latest release before the Jun-2025 build date). Evidence, obtained without reading any bidict source: the PyInstaller PYZ table of contents inside /workspace/dataset/test6_executable names exactly these modules — bidict, bidict._abc, bidict._base, bidict._bidict, bidict._dup, bidict._exc, bidict._frozen, bidict._iter, bidict._orderedbase, bidict._orderedbidict, bidict._typing, bidict.metadata. There is no bidict._named (namedbidict) and no bidict._delegating; both existed in 0.22.x and were removed in 0.23.0. Target the 0.23 contract: namedbidict and FrozenOrderedBidict do NOT exist, and OnDup has two fields (key, val) with no legacy kv field.

[MINIMUM VIABLE for THIS script] Everything test6.py needs is: (1) build from an ordered literal {'a':1,'b':2,'c':3}; (2) `has(key)` on the forward direction; (3) an `.inv` object whose `has()` tests the values; (4) render the resulting JS boolean as Python does — `b ? 'True' : 'False'` plus '\n'. Nothing else in this contract is exercised, so keep the extra API in a separate module file and do not let it change these two lines of output.

[CRITICAL / PROVEN+INFER] Back the storage with `Map`, never a plain object. Python dict preserves insertion order for ALL key types; a JS plain object silently reorders integer-like keys ('1','2','3' float to the front in ascending numeric order). The inverse of this bidict is int-keyed (1,2,3), so a plain object would corrupt iteration/repr order of `b.inv` the moment any sibling script prints or iterates it. `Map` matches Python dict order semantics exactly for both insert and overwrite.

[CRITICAL / INFER] Python dict key identity is hash+__eq__, so 1, 1.0, True and Decimal(1) are the SAME key, and 0 == 0.0 == False. JS `Map` uses SameValueZero, where 1 and true are distinct while 0 and -0 collide. For a faithful module, key every entry by a canonical token from a `pykey(v)` function (e.g. bools and ints and floats with integral value all map to the same numeric token; str maps to 's:'+v) and keep the original object alongside for iteration/repr. In THIS script the forward keys are always str and the inverse keys always int, so a naive Map works — but `--val -0` (int('-0') == 0) already shows why numeric canonicalization must not introduce a -0/0 split.

[DOC] Constructor mirrors dict's signature: bidict(), bidict(mapping), bidict(iterable_of_pairs), bidict(**kw), bidict(mapping, **kw). Insertion order follows the argument order, with kwargs applied last.

[DOC] Uniqueness is the whole point: keys are unique (as in dict) AND values are unique. Construction from a mapping/iterable that contains a repeated VALUE raises ValueDuplicationError (documented doctest: `bidict({'one': 1, 'uno': 1})` -> ValueDuplicationError with the offending value as the message). Construction never raises for repeated KEYS from an iterable of pairs — the default key policy is DROP_OLD, so last-one-wins like dict.

[DOC] Duplication policy model: `OnDupAction` is an enum with members RAISE, DROP_OLD, DROP_NEW; `OnDup` is a 2-field record (key, val) of OnDupActions; the three exported presets are ON_DUP_DEFAULT = OnDup(key=DROP_OLD, val=RAISE), ON_DUP_RAISE = OnDup(RAISE, RAISE), ON_DUP_DROP_OLD = OnDup(DROP_OLD, DROP_OLD). In JS: plain frozen objects `{key:'DROP_OLD', val:'RAISE'}` plus exported string/symbol constants.

[DOC] Which method uses which policy: __init__, __setitem__, update and |= use the instance's `on_dup` class attribute, which defaults to ON_DUP_DEFAULT; put() and putall() default to ON_DUP_RAISE; forceput() and forceupdate() behave as ON_DUP_DROP_OLD and never raise. Subclasses may override `on_dup` to change the defaults (documented extension point) — expose it as an overridable field on the JS class, read at call time.

[DOC] Consequences of ON_DUP_DEFAULT for `b[k] = v`: overwriting an EXISTING KEY's value succeeds silently (dict-like); assigning a value that already belongs to a DIFFERENT key raises ValueDuplicationError. That asymmetry is the single most-cited bidict behaviour and must be preserved.

[DOC+INFER] Semantics of each action when a collision is detected: RAISE -> throw the matching DuplicationError and leave the bidict untouched; DROP_OLD -> delete the colliding existing item(s), then insert the new item; DROP_NEW -> leave the bidict untouched and return without error (silent skip). [INFER] When both the key and the value collide with two DIFFERENT existing items, the decision is taken from the `val` action: RAISE -> KeyAndValueDuplicationError; otherwise both old items are dropped (DROP_OLD) or the write is skipped (DROP_NEW). Verify this both-collide branch before relying on it.

[DOC] Exact exception hierarchy to mirror: BidictException extends Error/Exception; DuplicationError extends BidictException; KeyDuplicationError and ValueDuplicationError extend DuplicationError; KeyAndValueDuplicationError extends BOTH KeyDuplicationError and ValueDuplicationError. None of them subclass KeyError/ValueError. JS recipe: class chain KeyAndValueDuplicationError extends KeyDuplicationError, plus `static [Symbol.hasInstance]` on ValueDuplicationError that also accepts KeyAndValueDuplicationError instances.

[INFER — verify if any sibling script lets a duplication error escape] Message payloads: ValueDuplicationError is constructed with the offending value (so str() is `repr`-ish of that value), KeyDuplicationError with the offending key, KeyAndValueDuplicationError with (key, value) so str() renders as a tuple `('a', 2)`. The uncaught-traceback header line is most likely `bidict._exc.ValueDuplicationError: 1` (full dotted module path, since bidict does not appear to rewrite __module__); the less likely alternative is bare `bidict.ValueDuplicationError`. Do not hardcode either without a probe that actually triggers it.

[DOC] update() and putall() are atomic / fail-clean: if any item in the batch triggers a RAISE, NOTHING from that batch is applied. Implement by validating the whole batch (against a scratch copy or a two-pass dedup) before mutating — a naive JS loop that applies items until it throws would leave half-applied state and diverge.

[DOC] Full mutable surface to expose on the bidict class: __setitem__/set, __delitem__/delete (KeyError if absent, and it must remove the pair from BOTH directions), put(key, val, onDup=ON_DUP_RAISE), forceput(key, val), putall(items, onDup=ON_DUP_RAISE), update(...), forceupdate(...), pop(key[, default]) (KeyError if absent and no default), popitem(), clear(), setdefault(key, default), copy(), and the PEP-584 merge operators (`|` returning a new bidict, `|=` behaving like update) added in 0.22. [INFER] setdefault inserts via the instance on_dup, so setdefault(newKey, existingValue) raises ValueDuplicationError rather than silently returning.

[DOC] Read-only surface inherited from the Mapping ABC: __getitem__ (KeyError on miss), __contains__ (KEYS ONLY), __iter__ (keys, insertion order), __len__, keys(), values(), items(), get(key, default=None), ==/!=, repr, bool (empty is falsy), and __reversed__ (all bidicts are reversible in 0.22+). Also `inverted(b)` as a module-level generator of (value, key) pairs, and the `__inverted__` protocol method.

[DOC] `b.inverse` is the canonical name and `b.inv` is the documented short alias — export BOTH as accessors on the JS class, since sibling scripts may use either. `b.inverse.inverse is b` and `b.inv.inv is b` are identity guarantees; `type(b.inv) is type(b)` for bidict, frozenbidict and OrderedBidict. Simplest faithful JS design: construct the pair eagerly and cross-link (`fwd._inv = inv; inv._inv = fwd`) sharing the two underlying Maps by reference so every mutation is visible from both sides. [INFER] Real bidict builds the inverse lazily and caches it (strong ref forward, weakref back) purely to avoid reference cycles; that is invisible at the API level, and `b.inv is b.inv` holds either way.

[DOC] len(b) == len(b.inv) always, and iterating b.inv yields the values of b as its keys, mapping back to b's keys — i.e. the inverse's items() is b's items() with each pair reversed, in the SAME order as the inverse's own insertion order (which is not necessarily b's key order after overwrites).

[CRITICAL / INFER] Order bookkeeping on overwrite — the case a naive port gets wrong. `b['a'] = 9` when 'a' already maps to 1 must (i) assign in the forward Map, leaving 'a' at its ORIGINAL position, and (ii) delete 1 from the inverse Map and insert 9, which lands 9 at the END of the inverse's order. Implement exactly as fwd.set(k,v) + inv.delete(oldVal) + inv.set(v,k); never rebuild the inverse from scratch, which would reorder it. Same rule for DROP_OLD drops: delete the displaced item(s) first, then insert, so the new key appends at the tail.

[DOC] Equality is order-insensitive and works against ANY Mapping, including plain dicts: bidict({'a':1}) == {'a':1} is True, and the reflected comparison dict == bidict is also True. Comparison against a non-mapping returns NotImplemented, i.e. False. In JS, implement an `equals(other)` that accepts a bidict, a Map, or a plain object, comparing size then key-by-key with Python key/value equivalence — and remember JS `==`/`===` can never be overloaded, so any ported script that compared with `==` must be rewritten to call equals().

[DOC] Type inventory to provide: bidict (mutable, unordered-by-contract but insertion-ordered in practice), frozenbidict (immutable and HASHABLE — hash is derived from the items, order-insensitively, like a frozenset of pairs), OrderedBidict (mutable, order-aware extras), plus the abstract BidirectionalMapping / MutableBidirectionalMapping ABCs whose defining feature is the abstract `inverse` property. bidict and OrderedBidict are UNHASHABLE (TypeError on hash()).

[DOC] OrderedBidict extras beyond bidict: move_to_end(key, last=True) (and it works on the inverse too, i.e. b.inverse.move_to_end(value)), popitem(last=True) with the OrderedDict-style `last` keyword, and equals_order_sensitive(other). Its `==` remains order-insensitive. Plain bidict's popitem() takes no `last` argument. [INFER] plain bidict.popitem() removes the most recently inserted item (dict.popitem is LIFO), so JS should pop the last Map entry, not the first.

[DOC] The abstract contract says plain `bidict` makes NO ordering guarantee, while in the CPython implementation it is dict-backed and therefore insertion-ordered; OrderedBidict is the type you use when order is part of your contract. For a JS port, always behave insertion-ordered (that is what the frozen executable actually does) — but do not rely on ordering for anything the observable output depends on unless the Python side is OrderedBidict.

[INFER] repr format: `f'{ClassName}({dict_literal})'`, with the empty case degenerating to no braces at all — repr(bidict()) == 'bidict()' and repr(bidict({'a':1,'b':2})) == "bidict({'a': 1, 'b': 2})". Inner rendering uses Python repr for keys and values ('a' single-quoted, ints bare), separated by ', '. print(b) falls through to the same text since there is no separate __str__. Subclass reprs use the subclass name. OrderedBidict uses the same dict-literal form in 0.22+ rather than the old list-of-pairs form.

[DOC/INFER] Not available on bidict, unlike dict: there is no fromkeys() classmethod (it would violate value uniqueness for 2+ keys) — attribute access raises AttributeError. bidicts ARE copyable and picklable (copy(), deepcopy, pickle round-trip preserving the inverse link). [INFER] __contains__ with an unhashable argument propagates TypeError from the underlying dict; irrelevant here because keys are always str.

[OUTPUT-FIDELITY / PROVEN] The script prints the raw bools, so the port's only rendering rule is Python's bool str: 'True'/'False', capital first letter, no quotes, each followed by '\n'. Total stdout is 10 bytes for True/True, 11 for mixed, 12 for False/False. stderr must stay EMPTY and the exit code 0 for every valid-argument case probed — bidict itself never wrote to stderr in any of the 25 runs.
